routes.description: Establish the anti-realist burden by denying that realism enjoys a defensible common-sense, historical, or semantic presumption and by showing that a substantive anti-realist alternative survives the principal conceptual objections raised against it.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the alleged realist advantages depend on unreliable attribution, contested semantic assumptions, or projection of specialist categories, while anti-realism remains a coherent position with consequences distinguishable from rival relativist accounts.

motionBridge.description: Show that common-sense, historical, and semantic considerations do not establish a presumptive advantage for moral realism over anti-realism.

centralBridges.description: Establish that ordinary or remembered pre-philosophical outlooks cannot reliably be classified using determinate contemporary metaethical categories.
Show that historical convergence claims must overcome projection, translation, source-selection, cultural-contact, and specialist-competence problems.
Articulate a genuinely metaethical anti-realist alternative whose semantic and practical commitments remain distinct from agent-relative obligation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Specify what surveys, linguistic use, memory, and behavior can establish about moral thought without treating them as direct tests of moral reality.
Show that interpretive or epistemic mediation does not uniquely discredit anti-realist positions when comparable access problems arise elsewhere.

routes.description: Establish the realist burden by defending common-sense or historical evidence for an objective conception of value and by showing that the proposed anti-realist distinctions do not defeat the resulting realist presumption.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if suitably competent pre-philosophical or cross-era sources provide credible evidence of objective-value commitments and if the anti-realist alternative either collapses into a perspectival variant or fails to displace that evidential presumption.

motionBridge.description: Show that common-sense, historical, or semantic evidence supplies moral realism with a meaningful presumptive advantage over anti-realism.

centralBridges.description: Identify a defensible common-sense evidential population despite the limitations of unreflective street-level surveys and raw response variation.
Establish that sufficiently comparable philosophical or intellectual traditions converge on objectively intended value claims despite substantive disagreement.
Show that agent and appraiser relativism share an underlying perspectival structure sufficient to limit the claimed semantic or metaphysical contrast.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Account for heterogeneous reports through competence, motivation, ignorance, or other factors that need not undermine an initial realist seeming.
Explain how an agent's interpretation of external standards bears on the claimed practical separation between relativist positions.

sections.title: Empirical Semantics and Metaphysical Scope
sections.rationale: The parties must delimit what evidence about linguistic use, psychology, surveys, or behavior can establish about ordinary meaning and whether any such finding bears directly on moral reality.

sections.title: Common Sense and Pre-Theoretical Outlooks
sections.rationale: A claimed common-sense advantage depends on identifying competent evidence of pre-theoretical commitments and resolving whether memory, reflection, pragmatic effects, and response variation permit reliable attribution.

sections.title: Historical Convergence and Metaethical Attribution
sections.rationale: The historical branch of the motion turns on whether cross-era intellectual traditions provide comparable evidence of objective-value commitments despite projection, translation, source-selection, and cultural-independence concerns.

sections.title: Agent and Appraiser Relativism
sections.rationale: The conceptual viability of the anti-realist alternative depends on whether these forms of relativism differ in semantic, metaphysical, and normative structure or merely redescribe one perspectival position.

sections.title: Normative Conflict and Epistemic Mediation
sections.rationale: Conflicting standards and first-person interpretation test the practical implications of the relativist distinction and whether access limitations create a distinctive problem for anti-realism.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: An empirical metaethical methodology is unstable if it relies on ordinary speakers as evidence about moral language while treating those speakers as confused about the concepts under investigation.
moves.attributionBasis: The surrounding exchange identifies Derek as the questioner addressing Lance directly and presenting the methodological challenge.

response.rationale: This is a constructive methodological challenge, so no earlier opposing move supplies a response component to assess.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly frames a material methodological tension but develops the alleged inconsistency only briefly.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological objection is recoverable, although reliance on speakers and treating speakers as confused are somewhat compressed notions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The point is advanced as a methodological question rather than as a demonstrated contradiction, fitting the limited support supplied.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A genuine tension is identified, but the inference assumes without full defense that empirical reliance and conceptual error attribution are incompatible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The challenge accurately invokes the opponent's empirical method, but it supplies no representative methodological evidence or comparison of compatible approaches.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly challenges calibration of empirical methods used to attribute ordinary moral concepts.

representationalCharity.rationale: No sufficiently developed competing interpretation is handled in this short methodological challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies empirical self-report research and presses whether treating respondents as conceptually confused destabilizes that methodology.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Empirical inquiry can establish what non-philosophers think or mean, but it cannot directly determine whether stance-independent moral facts exist.
moves.attributionBasis: Lance answers Derek's explicit methodological question and develops the distinction continuously until Derek acknowledges it.

components.text: Whether empirical evidence about speakers is being mistaken for direct evidence about stance-independent moral facts.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses an equivocation between empirical questions about speakers' thought or meaning and the metaphysical question whether stance-independent facts exist; that distinction defeats the alleged methodological inconsistency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies and resolves the decisive scope confusion underlying the methodological challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The empirical and metaphysical questions are expressly distinguished, with a clear limitation on what direct inquiry can establish.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical scope distinction is appropriately limited to direct empirical determination and does not deny indirect relevance.

charity.alternative: Empirical evidence about linguistic use might indirectly support a metaphysical view without directly detecting moral facts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Indirect evidential relevance does not erase the distinction between semantic evidence and direct metaphysical inquiry.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The semantic-versus-metaphysical distinction is explicit, internally consistent, and directly resolves the strongest version of the methodological objection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is principally conceptual and well explained, though it does not examine difficult indirect inferences from language to metaphysics.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly specifies the proper evidential scope of empirical metaethical inquiry.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves empirical inquiry's legitimate semantic role while denying only the stronger direct-metaphysical inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly limits direct empirical inquiry to what non-philosophers think while separating that from the existence of stance-independent facts.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: If realism cannot claim to represent ordinary common sense, it loses a presumptive burden-of-proof advantage rather than direct evidence for its metaphysics.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows Derek's question about what realism would lose by abandoning cognitivist and semantic commitments.

components.text: What dialectical consequence follows if empirical inquiry fails to establish a determinate ordinary realist outlook.

response.rationale: The move justifies replacing a direct metaphysical demand with the motion-relevant question of presumptive advantage: failure to establish realism as common sense removes a burden-of-proof benefit without proving anti-realism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reframe preserves the legitimate evidential issue and states its bounded dialectical consequence with considerable clarity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes loss of a presumption from positive disproof of realist metaphysics.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted consequence is expressly dialectical and presumptive, matching the cited common-sense argument rather than overstating metaphysical results.

charity.alternative: Realism could retain independent metaphysical arguments even if it is not the ordinary default.
charity.decisiveQualification: The claim removes only the common-sense presumptive advantage, not every argument for realism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from failure of default-status evidence to loss of that particular presumption is explicit and does not infer anti-realism's truth.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The dialectical point is supported by explanation and identified literature, though the prevalence and strength of the alleged realist presumption remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, it directly addresses whether common-sense considerations grant realism a presumptive advantage.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move explicitly preserves independent realist support and confines its conclusion to the disputed presumption.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt characterizes common-sense default status as a major realist dialectical asset and confines the consequence to presumptive argument.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Common-sense evidence for realism may be drawn from philosophers' remembered pre-philosophical outlooks rather than from wholly unreflective respondents unfamiliar with metaethical issues.
moves.attributionBasis: Derek explicitly develops a proposed alternative category and asks whether it has been recognized in the philosophical literature.

components.text: Whether a defensible evidential population can preserve realism's claimed pre-philosophical common-sense presumption.
Whether empirical inquiry can identify what people thought or meant without deciding metaphysical truth.

response.rationale: The proposal directly contacts the population problem by substituting philosophers' remembered pre-philosophical outlooks for unreflective street respondents, while remaining within the conceded empirical scope.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive evidential-population issue but leaves retrospective reliability and selection effects unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed population is clear, but the boundary of 'pre-philosophical' and the relevant level of later competence remain partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker proposes a possible evidential category rather than claiming it has already been validated, which fits the support.

charity.alternative: Unreflective respondents may be better evidence of ordinary common sense because later philosophers' memories are reconstructed.
charity.decisiveQualification: The proposed population gains conceptual competence but incurs retrospective-memory and selection costs.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The competence-based substitution is intelligible, but it leaves a material bridge from later philosophical competence to reliable earlier self-attribution.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The proposal relies on remembered outlooks and illustrative philosophical reactions without evidence that such memories are representative or reliable.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly proposes a defensible population for common-sense evidence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly recognizes the weakness of uninformed polling, though it does not yet address the strongest retrospective objection.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt proposes surveying philosophers about their views before philosophical study as an alternative to surveying wholly uninformed respondents.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Variation in reported moral outlooks may reflect incompetence, motivated ignorance, or other human complexities, so street-level surveys need not defeat an individual's initial realist seeming.
moves.attributionBasis: Derek takes the floor after Lance's methodological discussion and develops several explanations for variance before stating the limited evidential consequence.

components.text: Whether heterogeneous reports necessarily remove the evidential force of an individual's initial realist seeming.
What limited evidential conclusion variation in empirical reports can support.

response.rationale: The move contacts the variation-based challenge by supplying incompetence, motivation, and ignorance as rival explanations and drawing only the limited conclusion that variation need not defeat an initial seeming.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive issue but offers possibilities rather than a comparative account showing which explanation best fits the variation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited defeater claim is clear, though 'initial realist seeming' and the proposed human complexities are not sharply specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move argues that alternative explanations may exist and need not defeat a seeming, appropriately matching its speculative evidence.

charity.alternative: Observed variation may genuinely reflect diverse metaethical commitments rather than incompetence or motivated ignorance.
charity.decisiveQualification: Merely possible rival explanations do not establish that variation lacks evidential weight.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Possible rival causes coherently block a necessary inference from variation, but they do not establish the stronger credibility of realist seemings.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Incompetence, willful ignorance, and motivational explanations are asserted speculatively without representative evidence or comparative explanatory testing.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly supplies alternative explanations for heterogeneous common-sense reports.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move leaves the variation interpretation live but does not comparatively test it against the proposed competence and motivation explanations.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists willful ignorance, motivational resistance, and human complexity as explanations for variance and states a limited non-defeat conclusion.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: A pre-theoretical stance on a theoretical metaethical question may be conceptually unstable, and retrospective reports are unreliable because memory can reconstruct or confabulate earlier commitments.
moves.attributionBasis: Lance states his own position, develops the memory objection, and then adds structural problems with open-ended and forced-choice surveys.

components.text: Whether philosophers' retrospective reports can reliably identify their own determinate pre-philosophical metaethical commitments.
Whether speculative explanations of variation overcome the epistemic limits affecting self-reports.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses two failures in the proposed population: theoretical categories may not describe genuinely pre-theoretical stances, and reconstructive memory undermines retrospective attribution. It does not comparatively answer the separate rival explanations for variation.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly defeats the proposed retrospective population on conceptual and epistemic grounds, while leaving a secondary variation argument untreated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conceptual and memory-based objections are separately recoverable and appropriately limited to retrospective classification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Known reconstructive-memory concerns support substantial caution, though saying the category makes no conceptual sense is stronger than the excerpt establishes.

charity.alternative: People can hold implicit commitments before learning the technical labels later used to describe them.
charity.decisiveQualification: Possible implicit commitments still require reliable evidence that later memories track those earlier commitments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The memory objection is strong and explicit; the claim that every pre-theoretical stance on a theoretical question is conceptually incoherent is less fully defended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The appeal to reconstructive-memory research supplies a relevant warrant, but no specific findings or comparison with alternative retrospective methods are developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the reliability of classifying remembered pre-philosophical outlooks.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows that earlier people may have relevant views but correctly retains the decisive attribution and memory qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt separates conceptual instability from an epistemic problem and invokes memory research showing reconstruction and unreliability in retrospective reports.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Empirical investigation of moral language presupposes a contestable language-as-use account of meaning rather than a purely external account of linguistic patterns.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person discussion of the dissertation's empirical and metaphilosophical commitments matches Lance Bush's established position.

components.text: Whether empirical study of speech can coherently inform moral semantics under an articulated theory of meaning.

response.rationale: The move contacts the methodological tension by explaining that empirical speech-pattern research operates within a contestable language-as-use framework, rather than functioning as theory-neutral access to meaning.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies the missing methodological framework but does not fully compare it with the externalist alternative described.

precisionFindings.rationale: The theory-dependence claim is recoverable, although the contrast between use-based meaning and an external pattern account remains compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents the use theory as a contestable metaphilosophical commitment and does not claim that empirical patterns settle meaning independently.

charity.alternative: An external account of linguistic patterns could explain competent usage without relying on speakers' reflective semantic judgments.
charity.decisiveQualification: Pattern adequacy and speaker understanding may answer different methodological questions, so external description does not automatically settle meaning.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dependence of empirical interpretation on a theory of meaning is coherent, with one bounded bridge about why use is preferable to external pattern description.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies a concrete rival linguistic methodology but offers limited evidence for selecting the use-based account.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it materially specifies the theoretical assumptions governing empirical evidence about language.

representationalCharity.rationale: The externalist approach is presented as a serious rival, though the decisive comparison between explanatory aims remains abbreviated.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts externally modeled speech patterns with an account concerned with whether those patterns map onto speaker meaning and understanding.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Historically diverse religious and philosophical traditions often disagreed about substantive norms while sharing an objective conception of value, providing a presumptive historical advantage for realism.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly addresses Lance and introduces C. S. Lewis's historical convergence case from an explicitly realist perspective.

response.rationale: This constructive move advances an historical case for a realist presumption and therefore has no earlier response component to assess.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it provides a clear historical convergence thesis and diverse examples, though independence and classification warrants remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The convergence claim is recoverable, but objective value, realism, and the range of traditions are not consistently delimited.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples make convergence plausible, but the move somewhat overstates how directly diverse traditions establish a shared realist interpretation.

charity.alternative: Traditions can share normative seriousness or categorical language without sharing contemporary stance-independent realism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical convergence requires semantic and metaphysical comparability, not merely substantive moral commitment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Shared objective-value commitment could support a realist presumption, but the bridge from heterogeneous traditions to one comparable metaethical category remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several traditions are named, yet their texts, independence, representativeness, translations, and strongest nonrealist interpretations are not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the motion tier, the move directly argues that historical evidence supplies realism with a presumptive advantage.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move acknowledges substantive disagreement but does not adequately handle the strongest classification alternative concerning objective-value language.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes Aristotelian, Platonist, Daoist, Jewish, Christian, and other traditions as sharing objective value despite normative disagreement.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Because contemporary metaethical categories are historically recent, projecting them backward risks anachronistically misclassifying earlier thinkers and cultures as realists or anti-realists.
moves.attributionBasis: The answer follows McAllister's direct question and develops Bush's characteristic skepticism about attributing determinate metaethical views.

components.text: Whether earlier traditions can be validly classified under recent and technically specific realist or anti-realist categories.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the historical inference's classification problem: contemporary categories may be projected backward, and apparent metaethical overtones do not by themselves establish determinate category membership.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive attribution bridge while preserving the possibility that some earlier thinkers held recognizably relevant views.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anachronism objection is clearly limited and expressly avoids claiming that no historical person could hold a realist or relativist view.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move advances a risk of misclassification rather than universal historical agnosticism and supplies explicit counterexamples and caveats.

charity.alternative: Historical thinkers need not use modern labels to instantiate the commitments those labels now identify.
charity.decisiveQualification: Attribution still requires textual evidence for the relevant semantic or metaphysical commitments rather than thematic resemblance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between possible historical realism and unjustified wholesale projection is explicit and directly undermines the convergence inference's broad classification step.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual history point and qualified examples support caution, though the move does not examine the cited traditions individually.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports the historical-attribution bridge by identifying anachronistic classification risk.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply explicitly accepts that some earlier remarks may instantiate relevant views while retaining the decisive evidential requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt warns against projecting recent categories backward while conceding that passages such as Thrasymachus in Plato may have recognizable metaethical overtones.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Restricting historical evidence to recorded philosophical and intellectual systems still reveals broad convergence toward realist interpretations of value claims despite substantive normative disagreement.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker responds appreciatively to Lance, then reformulates Lewis's argument from the acknowledged realist side of the exchange.

components.text: Whether restricting evidence to articulated philosophical and intellectual systems supplies adequate grounds for comparable realist attribution.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the attribution concern by narrowing the population to recorded systems and listing traditions whose value claims appear realist, but it does not establish semantic comparability or answer projection directly.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive issue through population restriction, yet leaves the strongest anachronism and interpretation demands substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The narrowed evidential population is identifiable, but 'every single one,' 'realist perspective,' and the geographic scope remain insufficiently qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A broad claim about every listed system exceeds the illustrative support and omits material uncertainty about translation and interpretation.

charity.alternative: Recorded systems may employ objective-sounding normative discourse while differing fundamentally in semantics and metaphysics.
charity.decisiveQualification: Restricting the population improves competence but does not itself demonstrate comparable realist commitments.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Population restriction is relevant, but the inference from recorded normative systems to common realism retains a material classification and comparability bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The list of Stoic, Epicurean, Hindu, Daoist, and Confucian systems is selective and unsupported by specific representative texts or rival interpretations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports historical convergence using a narrowed population of articulated systems.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response narrows the evidence responsibly but largely assumes away the strongest interpretive alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists multiple recorded Western and Eastern systems and claims they appear to assume realism about value statements.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Translation problems, non-equivalent normative vocabularies, and later cultural contact undermine confident claims that independent traditions converged historically on moral realism.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker answers the request to assess Lewis's evidence and reiterates Bush's thesis that ordinary people commonly lack metaethical views.

components.text: Whether the listed traditions use comparable normative concepts and independently support a shared historical realist interpretation.
Whether broad cross-tradition agreement establishes objective-value convergence despite translation and contact effects.

response.rationale: The reply identifies translation, lexical non-equivalence, and cultural contact as failures in the convergence inference and states why merely listing traditions cannot establish independent, comparable realist commitments.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive comparability and independence demands, though concrete tradition-by-tradition demonstrations are limited.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limitations are separately identified and appropriately framed as constraints on confident convergence claims rather than proof of divergence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker repeatedly marks uncertainty and uses the considerations to undermine confidence rather than assert a universal absence of convergence.

charity.alternative: Shared value commitments can persist despite imperfect translation and historical contact among traditions.
charity.decisiveQualification: The realist case still must show that translated concepts are metaethically comparable and not products of dependent transmission.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Translation, conceptual non-equivalence, and non-independence each directly weaken the evidential inference, with only limited development of their application to named traditions.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies relevant cross-cultural lexical research and methodological problems, but gives few specific findings or historical contact pathways.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks the comparability and independence requirements for historical convergence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply leaves possible convergence open while clearly stating the additional evidence needed to support it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt raises culture-dependent moral lexicons, difficulty mapping terminology, current cross-cultural lexicalization research, and cultural-contact concerns.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: The distinction between agent and appraiser relativism may be structurally limited because a person can alternate between, and simultaneously occupy, the roles of acting and appraising.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker admits making the omission in his earlier realist teaching video and asks Lance to defend the distinction, identifying Derek McAllister.

components.text: Whether perspective dependence, rather than cultural classification alone, reveals a common structure across relativist positions.

response.rationale: The move shifts to the later conceptual issue and argues that agents also appraise and alternate roles. This is issue-bearing for the route but does not contact the historical convergence move's decisive demands.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It provides relevant contrary material for the broader debate but does not answer the selected earlier historical move's decisive component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The role-overlap claim is clear, though the inference from overlapping persons to equivalence of positions requires an unstated qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Role overlap is well motivated, but the claim that the distinction is merely epistemic exceeds what overlap alone establishes.

charity.alternative: The same person can occupy both roles while the semantic rule and source of obligation remain structurally different.
charity.decisiveQualification: Role overlap does not entail theoretical identity between agent-relative obligation and appraiser-indexed assertion.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The overlap premise is plausible, but inferring no ontological or substantive theoretical difference from personal role alternation is a material non sequitur.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary examples support role overlap, but the move supplies no analysis showing that overlap collapses the distinct semantic or normative structures.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports the claim that agent and appraiser relativism share one perspectival structure.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the distinction's intended role labels but does not preserve the strongest semantic and normative contrast.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that a person can be both agent and appraiser and characterizes the difference as whose perspective evaluates the act.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Agent relativism generates conflicting obligations when the standards of different agents or cultures authorize incompatible actions and demands.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted explanatory turn continues Bush's response and uses wallet-taking and cultural-intervention cases to expose conflicts.

components.text: Whether role overlap erases the distinctive normative conflicts generated when different agents' standards authorize incompatible demands.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the collapse argument by showing that agent relativism's externally interacting standards generate conflicting obligations, a structural consequence not established merely by noting that people also appraise.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly supplies a substantive difference overlooked by the role-overlap argument, though the conflict cases need further formal resolution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The individual and cultural versions of agent relativism and the resulting incompatible demands are described through concrete cases.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated standards in the examples, incompatible obligations follow; the move does not claim every possible agent-relative theory has identical wording.

charity.alternative: An agent relativist might specify priority, jurisdiction, or noninterference rules that resolve cross-agent conflicts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Such rules require additional structure not supplied merely by making obligation relative to each agent's standards.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The wallet and cultural-intervention cases make the incompatible-demand inference clear, with one bounded gap concerning how sophisticated agent relativism could add conflict rules.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete counterexamples appropriately support the conceptual claim, though no systematic survey of agent-relativist formulations is offered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly attacks collapse by identifying a distinctive normative structure of agent relativism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly treats agent relativism as potentially refinable while showing the challenge faced by the unqualified version under discussion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt develops individual and cultural cases in which different agents' standards authorize incompatible conduct and intervention demands.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Appraiser relativism gives moral assertions perspective-indexed descriptive content without imposing the externally generated obligations associated with agent relativism.
moves.attributionBasis: Bush explicitly contrasts appraiser relativism with the conflict cases he has just developed for agent relativism.

components.text: Whether alternating practical roles entails that agent and appraiser relativism have the same semantic and normative commitments.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses why role overlap does not collapse the theories: appraiser relativism indexes assertion content to a perspective, whereas agent relativism generates obligations from an agent's standards.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the semantic and normative dimensions that the role-overlap objection conflates.

precisionFindings.rationale: Perspective-indexed content and externally generated obligation are expressly contrasted without shifting the meanings of the two positions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The contrast follows from the definitions and examples used in the exchange and is not extended beyond those specified theories.

charity.alternative: Both theories remain perspectival because truth or obligation ultimately depends on some standpoint.
charity.decisiveQualification: Shared perspective dependence does not eliminate differences in asserted content or in who is normatively bound.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move clearly separates semantic content from normative consequence and directly resolves the equivocation between personal roles and theoretical structures.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual contrast is defended through the preceding conflict cases, with only a bounded need for fuller formal semantics.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly articulates the coherent semantic and practical distinction required by the anti-realist alternative.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the common perspectival feature while explaining why it is insufficient for theoretical collapse.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that critiques of agent relativism concern its normative conflict, while appraiser relativism makes a different perspective-indexed semantic claim.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Appraiser relativism is a genuine metaethical position with semantic and metaphysical commitments, rather than merely a description of variation among moral practices.
moves.attributionBasis: Bush begins with an explicit clarification and distinguishes descriptive relativism from appraiser relativism's semantic and metaphysical theses.

components.text: Whether appraiser relativism is merely a description of varying practices rather than a genuine semantic and metaphysical position.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the conflation of descriptive variation with appraiser relativism by explaining that the latter can hold even for one person and includes semantic and metaphysical commitments.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly defeats the descriptive-only interpretation through a decisive one-person counterexample and category comparison.

precisionFindings.rationale: Descriptive relativism, appraiser relativism, semantics, and metaphysical implications are consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The metaethical classification follows from the specified semantic and metaphysical commitments and is carefully distinguished from descriptive variation.

charity.alternative: Appraiser relativism may look sociological because its truth conditions refer to appraisers' standards and practices.
charity.decisiveQualification: Dependence on a standpoint is compatible with a genuine semantic thesis about assertion content and metaphysical truth conditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The one-person case decisively separates actual variation from the semantic thesis, and the metaethical classification follows coherently.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual comparison with error theory and naturalist realism supports classification, though the metaphysical implications are only briefly elaborated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly establishes that the proposed alternative is genuinely metaethical and semantically substantive.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply squarely addresses the strongest descriptive interpretation without denying the theory's practical or psychological applications.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explains that appraiser relativism could hold without interpersonal variation and locates it among views defined by semantic and metaphysical commitments.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: Even when agent and appraiser relativism are both properly metaethical, they may remain forms of one underlying relativism differentiated chiefly by the perspective from which evaluation occurs.
moves.attributionBasis: McAllister explicitly clarifies his earlier wording and develops an extended perspectival analogy before asking whether his interpretation is correct.

components.text: Whether distinct semantic and normative implementations nevertheless share enough perspective dependence to count as one underlying relativism.
Whether recognizing appraiser relativism as properly metaethical answers the proposed underlying structural similarity.
Whether agent relativism's distinctive conflict consequences prevent a broader perspectival classification.

response.rationale: The reply concedes appraiser relativism's proper metaethical status and contacts the semantic contrast by proposing a common perspectival genus, but it does not answer the distinctive normative-conflict consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive common-structure issue but only partially addresses the semantic, metaphysical, and normative differences supporting the distinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The genus claim is recoverable, but 'perspective' shifts among evaluator, truth index, and source of obligation without full stabilization.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents the collapse as a tentative interpretation and concedes correct classification, though perspective alone underwarrants the claimed limitation.

charity.alternative: Agent and appraiser relativism can share a broad relativist genus while differing importantly in semantics, metaphysics, and normative consequences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Common perspective dependence establishes family resemblance, not identity or dialectical insignificance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A common perspectival genus is coherent, but the inference that this leaves little valuable difference overlooks the previously articulated semantic and normative contrasts.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The perspectival analogy supports family resemblance, but no formal account shows that it subsumes the distinct truth and obligation structures.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the central tier, it directly supports the realist route's proposed collapse of the two relativist positions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move concedes proper metaethical status but still compresses the strongest multidimensional distinction into perspective alone.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt acknowledges both positions as relativism and appraiser relativism as properly metaethical, then identifies perspective as their alleged sole important difference.

moves.speaker: Derek McAllister
moves.proposition: External cultural standards can bind an agent only as the agent understands those standards, so first-person epistemic mediation restores a structural similarity between agent and appraiser relativism.
moves.attributionBasis: McAllister acknowledges Bush's explanation and then introduces a distinct epistemic route to his continuing collapse argument.

components.text: Whether external agent-relative standards remain structurally distinct once every agent accesses them through first-person interpretation.
Whether epistemic interpretation converts a metaethical semantic position into the same structure as agent-relative obligation.
Whether first-person mediation resolves conflicting externally generated demands.

response.rationale: The move contacts the semantic contrast by arguing that external standards are always interpreted from the agent's perspective, but it leaves untouched the difference between epistemic access, truth conditions, and normative source.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive perspective issue but does not answer the separate semantic and normative components of the distinction.

precisionFindings.rationale: The mediation thesis is clear, but 'perspective' again conflates an epistemic viewpoint with a semantic index and normative authority.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It plausibly establishes interpretive mediation, but the proposed collapse exceeds that epistemic premise without a further bridge.

charity.alternative: An agent can interpret external standards fallibly while those standards remain external sources of obligation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic mediation concerns access and does not by itself change the standards' metaphysical or normative source.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The access premise is plausible, but inferring structural collapse from first-person interpretation equivocates between epistemic mediation and constitutive perspective dependence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The solipsistic and cultural examples illustrate mediated understanding, though they do not establish the stronger semantic or metaphysical conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly explains how first-person interpretation bears on external agent-relative standards.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes external standards but insufficiently preserves the strongest distinction between access to them and constitution by perspective.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that an agent is bound by other cultures' codes only as the agent understands them and treats that mediation as perspectival collapse.

moves.speaker: Lance Bush
moves.proposition: Epistemic mediation is not distinctive to agent relativism and does not make it false, because moral realist views face comparable limitations on access to relevant facts or standards.
moves.attributionBasis: Bush immediately rejects the proposed distinctive problem, compares realism's epistemic access, and warns against consequence-based rejection.

components.text: Whether first-person epistemic access uniquely collapses agent relativism into appraiser relativism or otherwise counts against its truth.
Whether generic perspective dependence eliminates the semantic and normative distinction between the positions.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the inference's failure by separating epistemic access from truth and showing that comparable access limitations can arise for realism; therefore mediation is neither distinctive nor a collapse argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the access-versus-truth error and directly supplies the parity consequence that defeats the proposed inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply consistently distinguishes epistemic access, metaphysical truth, and the limited exceptions available to acquaintance or self-evidence theories.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The non sequitur claim is well supported and explicitly qualified by noting realist theories that claim direct acquaintance or self-evidence.

charity.alternative: Some realist theories claim self-evident or directly acquainted moral facts and thus avoid the same access problem.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even those exceptions do not show that mediated access makes agent relativism false or semantically identical to appraiser relativism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between epistemic limitation and falsity is explicit, and the parity comparison directly defeats the inference from mediation to theoretical collapse.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual parity argument is well supported by identified realist access variants, with only a bounded absence of fuller epistemological comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within the subsidiary tier, it directly supports epistemic parity by showing that mediated access is not uniquely anti-realist.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply expressly states the strongest realist exception and explains why it does not rescue the collapse inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares agent relativism's access problem with realist access to facts, notes acquaintance and self-evidence exceptions, and denies that access difficulty implies falsity.
